title: Operation Black Buck
sub: Long-range Vulcan raids from Ascension Island

markers.label: RAF Ascension Island
markers.description: Ascension Island was the staging base for the Vulcan bombers and Victor tankers that made the extraordinary round trip possible.

markers.label: Port Stanley airfield
markers.description: Black Buck targeted Stanley's runway to restrict Argentine air operations and signal that Britain could strike the occupied islands.

slides.title: A Bomber Route Across the Atlantic
slides.cap: RAF Vulcan imagery associated with the Black Buck raids.
slides.body: Operation Black Buck sent RAF Vulcan bombers from Ascension Island to attack the runway at Port Stanley. The raids required complex chains of Victor tankers and became a test of range, planning, and endurance as much as bombing accuracy. Militarily, the runway damage was limited; strategically, the operation showed Argentina that the islands were within British reach and forced planners to consider the vulnerability of mainland-linked air operations.

markers.label: Government House, Stanley
markers.description: The small Royal Marine garrison resisted around Stanley before surrendering to a much larger Argentine landing force.

markers.label: Mullet Creek landing area
markers.description: Argentine units came ashore around Stanley, turning a long-running sovereignty dispute into an armed occupation.

slides.title: The Seizure That Started the War
slides.cap: An Argentine LVTP-7 amphibious vehicle of the type associated with Argentine marine landings.
slides.body: Operation Rosary was Argentina's 2 April 1982 invasion of the Falkland Islands. Argentine commanders expected a quick occupation to strengthen Buenos Aires's claim and perhaps avoid a major British response. Instead, the landing created a political crisis in London, rallied British public opinion, and forced both governments into a war neither side could easily de-escalate.

title: Invasion of South Georgia
sub: Argentina extends the crisis to South Georgia

markers.label: Grytviken
markers.description: Grytviken was the center of the brief British resistance and later an early target for British recapture.

markers.label: Leith Harbour
markers.description: The earlier scrap-metal workers dispute around Leith helped escalate tensions before the Argentine military landing.

slides.title: A Remote Island Becomes an Early Test
slides.body: Argentina's move on South Georgia widened the campaign beyond the Falklands themselves. The island had little immediate military value compared with East Falkland, but it mattered symbolically and operationally: retaking it would let Britain prove that the task force could fight, coordinate helicopters and ships in severe weather, and reverse Argentine gains before the main amphibious landing.

stats.val: Sets up Britain's first recapture operation

title: Operation Algeciras
sub: A covert Argentine plot near Gibraltar

markers.label: Gibraltar anchorage
markers.description: Argentine commandos planned to attack British naval targets with limpet mines near Gibraltar.

markers.label: Algeciras
markers.description: Spanish police disrupted the team before the planned attack could be carried out.

slides.title: The War's Covert European Edge
slides.cap: Image associated with Operation Algeciras and the wider Gibraltar plot.
slides.body: Operation Algeciras was Argentina's attempt to strike British shipping at Gibraltar with commandos and limpet mines. The plan failed after Spanish authorities uncovered the team, but the episode shows that the conflict was not confined to the South Atlantic. Argentina looked for asymmetric pressure points, while Britain had to think about port security, intelligence, and escalation far from the islands.

markers.label: Grytviken
markers.description: British forces accepted the Argentine surrender at Grytviken after disabling the submarine ARA Santa Fe.

markers.label: South Georgia approaches
markers.description: Bad weather, helicopter losses, and improvised special-forces movement shaped the operation.

slides.title: First British Success
slides.cap: South Georgia, the first territory retaken by British forces in the campaign.
slides.body: Operation Paraquet recaptured South Georgia and gave Britain its first clear victory of the campaign. The operation mixed special forces, naval aviation, ships, and rapid improvisation in harsh weather. Its military scale was smaller than the later Falklands landing, but the political effect was large: it proved the task force was not just sailing south, it was already reversing Argentine control.

stats.val: Boosts British morale before the Falklands landing

title: Battle of San Carlos
sub: The amphibious landing and Bomb Alley

markers.label: San Carlos Water
markers.description: British troops landed here to create the beachhead for the ground campaign across East Falkland.

markers.label: Falkland Sound
markers.description: Argentine aircraft attacked ships in the confined waters that British sailors called Bomb Alley.

slides.title: The Beachhead Under Air Attack
slides.cap: British troops advancing after the San Carlos landing.
slides.body: The Battle of San Carlos opened the land campaign. British troops got ashore, but the ships supporting them endured repeated low-level Argentine air attacks while unloading men, ammunition, vehicles, and supplies. Holding the anchorage made the advance on Stanley possible; the losses and damage to ships also made San Carlos one of the war's defining lessons in air defense, naval logistics, and amphibious risk.

stats.val: Amphibious success under heavy air attack

title: Battle of Goose Green
sub: 2 Para fights the first major land battle

markers.label: Goose Green
markers.description: The settlement and nearby Argentine garrison became the first major British land objective after San Carlos.

markers.label: Darwin
markers.description: The Darwin-Goose Green isthmus forced attackers through exposed ground under fire.

slides.title: Momentum on Land
slides.cap: Goose Green school, one of the recognizable sites from the battle area.
slides.body: Goose Green was the first major land battle after the British landing. 2 Para attacked over open ground against a larger Argentine garrison, and Lieutenant Colonel H. Jones was killed during the fighting. The British victory freed civilians, captured hundreds of prisoners, and gave the ground campaign momentum before the final advance toward Stanley.

title: 1982 British Army Gazelle Friendly Fire Incident
sub: Command-and-control failure in a crowded battlespace

markers.label: Pleasant Peak area
markers.description: A British Gazelle helicopter was mistakenly shot down by British forces, killing four servicemen.

markers.label: Stanley approaches
markers.description: The incident occurred as British forces were pushing toward the final battles around Stanley.

slides.title: A Small Incident With a Large Lesson
slides.cap: A British Army Gazelle helicopter, the aircraft type involved in the incident.
slides.body: The Gazelle friendly-fire incident exposed how hard identification can become when helicopters, ships, ground forces, and air defenses operate under stress. Four British servicemen were killed when a British helicopter was mistaken for hostile aircraft. The episode did not decide the campaign, but it belongs in the deep dive because it reveals the human cost of command friction and the limits of battlefield awareness.
